# Monitoring, Logging, and Alerting

## Overview
Once automations run unattended in production, you need to know they are actually working - silent failure is the enemy, and monitoring, logging, and alerting are how professionals stay in control. Monitoring means keeping an eye on the health of your automations: are they running on schedule, succeeding, and completing in reasonable time? The platforms provide run histories, but for anything important you set up your own visibility. Logging is the foundation: your workflow records meaningful events and outcomes - what it processed, what it decided, what succeeded or failed, and key data (without sensitive details) - typically to a Google Sheet, a database table, or a dedicated logging tool. Good logs turn 'something is wrong' into 'here is exactly what happened at 3:14 AM', which is the difference between a five-minute fix and hours of guesswork. From logs you can derive simple metrics and even a small dashboard: how many records processed today, success rate, error count - so you can spot trends like a rising failure rate before it becomes a crisis. The most important habit is proactive alerting: instead of discovering a broken automation days later when someone complains, the automation itself notifies you (via Slack, email, or SMS) the moment a failure or anomaly occurs - a run failed, no data arrived when it should have, or volume spiked unexpectedly. You also maintain an audit trail - a record of what the automation did and when - which matters for accountability, debugging, and compliance. Building monitoring and alerting into your automations from the start signals operational maturity and is precisely what makes an employer comfortable trusting you with mission-critical processes.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: Why monitoring matters in production; Logging events and outcomes; Success/failure metrics and dashboards; Proactive alerting on failures and anomalies; Audit trails and accountability. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
**Practical Task:** Add logging to an automation so each run records key outcomes to a sheet or database, then add an alert step that notifies you immediately if a run fails or produces no results.
**Mini Project:** Build a monitoring layer for one of your automations: log every run's status and metrics, create a simple daily health-summary (counts and success rate) sent to you, and configure real-time failure alerts to Slack or email.
**Assignment:** Explain the difference between logging, monitoring, and alerting, and describe three specific events you would alert on for a business-critical automation and why.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
